positions/amyraldism/oneLine: God first decreed that Christ should die for all on condition of faith, and then, since none would believe unaided, decreed to give faith to the elect.
positions/amyraldism/coreClaims/0: Christ’s atonement is universal in intent: he died sufficiently and conditionally for all.
positions/amyraldism/coreClaims/1: Because humanity is morally unable to believe, God also eternally elects some to receive effectual grace.
positions/amyraldism/coreClaims/2: The decree to provide redemption logically precedes the decree of election.
positions/amyraldism/coreClaims/3: The universal offer of the gospel is grounded in a real universal provision.
positions/amyraldism/origin: Developed by the Scottish theologian John Cameron at Saumur and his student Moïse Amyraut (Brief Traitté de la prédestination, 1634); opposed by the Helvetic Consensus (1675). English hypothetical universalists (Davenant, Ussher, Baxter) held related views.
positions/amyraldism/strongestArguments/: It honours both the universal texts and the particular texts of Scripture.
It grounds the free offer of the gospel in a genuine provision for all.
Defenders show that hypothetical universalism was represented among delegates at Dort and at Westminster.
positions/amyraldism/strongestObjections: Strict Calvinists: it introduces a frustrated divine intention and a disordered sequence of decrees.
Arminians: it still leaves the non-elect unable to benefit from the provision made for them.
Critics argue the universal decree is idle if it is never effective for anyone.
positions/amyraldism/responses/0: Amyraldians answer that Scripture itself speaks both of a love for the world and a special love for the elect.
positions/amyraldism/responses/1: They note that the Canons of Dort (II.3) affirm the death of Christ sufficient for the whole world.
positions/amyraldism/consequences/0: Tolerated within French Protestantism; controversial in Switzerland.
positions/amyraldism/consequences/1: Persisting as a minority Reformed and evangelical option.
positions/hyper-calvinism/oneLine: Because only the elect can or will respond, the gospel should not be offered indiscriminately to all, nor all called to a duty of saving faith.
positions/hyper-calvinism/coreClaims/0: God’s decrees are the controlling starting point; election and reprobation are emphasised.
positions/hyper-calvinism/coreClaims/1: There is no "free offer" of grace to sinners as such; the gospel is proclaimed but sensible sinners only are invited.
positions/hyper-calvinism/coreClaims/2: Saving faith is not the duty of the unregenerate ("no duty-faith").
positions/hyper-calvinism/coreClaims/3: Some held "eternal justification" of the elect.
positions/hyper-calvinism/origin: Emerged among English Independents and Particular Baptists c.1700, e.g. Joseph Hussey’s God’s Operations of Grace but No Offers of Grace (1707), and associated with John Brine and (debatedly) John Gill; challenged by Andrew Fuller’s The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation (1785).
positions/hyper-calvinism/strongestArgum: It claims logical consistency with particular redemption: it is incoherent to offer what was not provided.
It guards against "duty-faith" being turned into a work.
It protects God’s sovereignty in conversion.
positions/hyper-calvinism/strongestObjec: Mainstream Calvinists (Fuller, Spurgeon) argue it contradicts the universal commands to repent and believe (Acts 17:30).
It suppressed evangelism and missions, as Carey’s generation complained.
It confuses God’s secret will with his revealed will.
positions/hyper-calvinism/responses/0: Hyper-Calvinists answer that they do preach to all, but address invitations to those in whom the Spirit has produced a sense of need.
positions/hyper-calvinism/responses/1: Some historians argue Gill has been unfairly labelled and did urge sinners to repent.
positions/hyper-calvinism/consequences/0: Contributed to a decline of Particular Baptist evangelism in the 18th century.
positions/hyper-calvinism/consequences/1: Provoked Fullerism, which fed the Baptist Missionary Society (1792).
positions/wesleyan-entire-sanctification: Wesleyan holiness and entire sanctification
Christian perfection
second blessing
perfect love
Beyond justification, believers may by faith receive a second work of grace in this life — entire sanctification — in which love for God and neighbour fills the heart and casts out willful sin.
Prevenient grace is given to all; justification is by faith, ordinarily accompanied by the witness of the Spirit (assurance).
Sanctification begins at the new birth and grows; but a further instantaneous work of grace, received by faith, can cleanse the heart from inbred sin.
Perfection means perfect love, not freedom from ignorance, mistakes, infirmity or temptation.
Salvation can be lost through persistent unbelief.
Matthew 5:48
1 Thessalonians 5:23
1 John 1:7-9
1 John 3:9
Hebrews 6:1
Romans 8:16
Ezekiel 36:25-27

John Wesley (A Plain Account of Christian Perfection, 1766), drawing on Anglican, Pietist and Eastern patristic sources (Macarius); radicalised as "altar theology" by Phoebe Palmer (The Way of Holiness, 1843) and the 19th-century Holiness movement.
John Fletcher
Adam Clarke
Asa Mahan
Catherine and William Booth
Scripture commands and promises holiness in this life (1 Thess 5:23) and speaks of hearts cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9).
It holds high expectations of transformation instead of resigned sinfulness.
It produced social reform: abolition, women’s preaching, rescue missions.
Calvinists and Lutherans: indwelling sin remains to death (Rom 7; 1 John 1:8); perfectionism breeds either pride or despair.
Defining sin as "voluntary transgression of a known law" may trivialise sin.
Testimonies to instantaneous entire sanctification were often not borne out in life.
Wesleyans answer that perfection is relative and dynamic; it does not deny the need for Christ’s atonement moment by moment.
They distinguish sins proper from involuntary infirmities, which are covered by Christ’s blood.
Shaped Methodism, the Holiness churches (Church of the Nazarene, Wesleyan Church, Salvation Army) and early Pentecostal theology.
positions/keswick-higher-life/oneLine: A decisive crisis of full surrender and faith brings the believer into a life of rest and victory in which the indwelling Christ counteracts, though does not eradicate, the sinful nature.
positions/keswick-higher-life/coreClaims: Many Christians live "carnal" lives below their privileges.
Through consecration and the "rest of faith" one enters a higher life of habitual victory over known sin.
Sin’s tendency is counteracted by the Spirit, not eradicated (contrast Wesleyan eradication).
This is often linked with a "filling" or empowering of the Spirit for service.
positions/keswick-higher-life/origin: Emerged from the American Higher Life movement (William Boardman, 1858) and the British meetings of Robert Pearsall and Hannah Whitall Smith (Oxford 1874, Brighton 1875); annual Keswick Convention in the English Lake District from 1875.
positions/keswick-higher-life/strongestA: It speaks to Christians frustrated by defeat and offers a grace-based way to holiness.
It fuelled missionary dedication (many missionaries were recruited at Keswick).
It avoids Wesleyan claims to sinless perfection while affirming real victory.
positions/keswick-higher-life/strongestO: B. B. Warfield (Perfectionism, 1918-31): it is a quietist "let go and let God" that divides Christians into two classes.
J. I. Packer: it can produce passivity and disillusionment when promised victory does not come.
Wesleyans: it settles for counteraction rather than heart cleansing.
positions/keswick-higher-life/responses/: Keswick teachers answer that surrender is active trust and that growth continues after the crisis.
Later Keswick speakers moved toward a more Reformed, progressive view of sanctification.
positions/keswick-higher-life/consequenc: Shaped British and American evangelical spirituality, Christian and Missionary Alliance, and early Pentecostal language of "overcoming".
positions/finished-work-sanctification/o: Sanctification is accomplished in Christ’s finished work and given at conversion, then progressively appropriated; there is no separate second crisis of entire sanctification before Spirit baptism.
positions/finished-work-sanctification/c: Conversion includes justification and positional sanctification through identification with Christ.
Believers grow in holiness by continuing to reckon themselves dead to sin and alive to God.
The baptism in the Holy Spirit, evidenced by tongues, is the one subsequent experience.
The Wesleyan-Holiness three-stage order (conversion, sanctification, Spirit baptism) is rejected.
positions/finished-work-sanctification/o: Preached by William H. Durham at the 1910 Stone Church convention in Chicago; spread through Durham’s Los Angeles campaign (1911) and adopted by the Assemblies of God at its founding (1914).
positions/finished-work-sanctification/s: It locates holiness in Christ’s completed work rather than in a further human experience.
It simplified Pentecostal teaching and appealed to converts from Baptist and non-Wesleyan backgrounds.
Texts like Hebrews 10:14 speak of believers already sanctified.
Holiness Pentecostals (Church of God in Christ, Church of God [Cleveland], Pentecostal Holiness Church): it lowers the standard of heart purity.
Seymour and Parham opposed it; critics saw it as a return to Baptist "positional" holiness.
Some see it opening the door to the Oneness ("New Issue") schism.
positions/finished-work-sanctification/r: Finished Work Pentecostals answer that progressive sanctification is demanding and real.
They argue that a single subsequent experience better fits Acts.
positions/finished-work-sanctification/c: Divided Pentecostalism into Wesleyan (three-stage) and Finished Work (two-stage) families.
The latter, including the Assemblies of God, became the largest Pentecostal stream.
positions/free-grace-theology/oneLine: Eternal life is received simply by believing Jesus’ promise; repentance (as turning from sin), surrender to Christ’s lordship and perseverance in good works are not conditions of salvation or of assurance.
positions/free-grace-theology/coreClaims: Saving faith is persuasion that Jesus guarantees eternal life to the believer.
Discipleship and lordship are important but distinct from the free gift of salvation.
Assurance is of the essence of saving faith and rests on God’s promise, not on inspecting one’s works.
Believers who live carnally lose rewards, not salvation.
positions/free-grace-theology/origin: Rooted in dispensational teaching at Dallas Theological Seminary (Lewis Sperry Chafer); articulated by Zane Hodges (The Gospel Under Siege, 1981; Absolutely Free!, 1989) and Charles Ryrie (So Great Salvation, 1989); Grace Evangelical Society founded 1986.
positions/free-grace-theology/strongestA: It guards the gospel from any admixture of works and keeps grace free.
It gives assurance to struggling believers.
John’s Gospel, written that readers may believe and have life, names belief alone as the condition.
positions/free-grace-theology/strongestO: Lordship advocates: it produces "easy believism" and false assurance among the unregenerate.
It separates justification from regeneration and sanctification contrary to Romans 6 and James 2.
Its reduction of faith to assent ignores biblical calls to repentance.
positions/free-grace-theology/responses/: Free grace teachers answer that lordship theology makes assurance impossible and turns faith into commitment-as-work.
They hold that God disciplines believers and that the judgement seat of Christ has real consequences.
positions/free-grace-theology/consequenc: Divided American dispensationalists in the "lordship controversy" (1988-89).
